what_its_for: Selinexor is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of blood cancers. It is approved to treat multiple myeloma (a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Your doctor has prescribed this medicine because other treatments have not worked well enough or have stopped working.
how_to_take: Take selinexor by mouth as a tablet. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food or an anti-nausea medicine beforehand may help reduce stomach upset. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, break, or chew it. Try to take it at the same time on your scheduled dosing days each week. If you vomit after taking your dose, do NOT take another tablet — just wait until your next scheduled dose.
dosing: The dose your doctor prescribes will depend on your specific condition and treatment plan. A common dose is 80 mg taken once or twice a week, but your doctor may adjust this based on how you respond to the medicine and any side effects you experience. Always follow the exact schedule your doctor gives you. This medicine is often given together with other cancer medicines such as dexamethasone and/or bortezomib.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you miss a full day, skip that missed dose completely and take your next dose on the normally scheduled day. Do NOT take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store selinexor tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep them away from moisture, heat, and direct sunlight. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicines down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to safely dispose of leftover medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy, confused, or mentally foggy, as selinexor can affect your ability to think clearly. Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink plenty of fluids unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking any new medicines, including vitamins, supplements, or herbal products, as some may interact with selinexor. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay. Women who could become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 week after the last dose. Men with female partners who could become pregnant should also use contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience any of the following: severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; signs of low sodium levels such as confusion, memory problems, muscle weakness, or seizures; signs of low blood cell counts such as unusual bleeding or bruising, fever, chills, or feeling very tired and short of breath; sudden vision changes, severe headache, or difficulty walking; signs of serious infection; significant weight loss or loss of appetite that is affecting your ability to eat; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you. These may be signs of serious side effects that need prompt medical attention.
when_it_works: Selinexor does not work overnight. It may take several weeks to months of treatment before your doctor can tell if the medicine is helping. Your doctor will check your progress with regular blood tests, imaging scans, and other evaluations. It is very important to keep all of your appointments even if you feel unwell. Do not stop taking selinexor without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel side effects.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Selinexor can harm an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Do not breastfeed while taking selinexor and for at least 1 week after your last dose. Older adults: Older patients (65 years and above) may be more sensitive to the side effects of selinexor, especially nausea, fatigue, and low sodium levels. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Children: Selinexor has not been approved for use in children.
